arc.scene1_hook: Open on a giant pill capsule splitting open at center frame — inside, the number "37%" pulses in red. A narrator says this drug barely gets into your blood. The pill dissolves downward, leaving the percentage hanging ominously. Below, a faint bloodstream river flows left-to-right with almost no drug particles visible — the visual says "failure." Label pill: "THE WORST DRUG?" at ZONE_TITLE.
arc.scene2_mystery: A simplified lung outline appears at center frame, glowing faintly. Tiny azithromycin dots drift through a bloodstream ribbon below — barely any reach the lung. A "blood level" bar on the left stays tiny. The lung looks undefended, bacteria dots multiply inside it. The visual question: if so little drug reaches the blood, how does this treat pneumonia? Label: "THE PROBLEM".
arc.scene3_wrong_answer: Show the "obvious" answer: maybe you just take a huge dose. A giant pile of pills stacks up at center. An arrow pumps more drug into the bloodstream river. But the blood-level bar barely moves — the drug vanishes from the blood almost as fast as it arrives. The pills keep piling but the lung bacteria keep multiplying. Brute force isn't working. Label: "MORE PILLS?"
arc.scene4_contradiction: The twist: a single immune cell (neutrophil shape — a blobby circle with a nucleus) drifts through the bloodstream. As it passes azithromycin molecules, it ABSORBS them — the dots disappear INTO the cell, which glows brighter and brighter blue. The cell is now packed with drug. It exits the bloodstream and enters the lung. Flash: "64-98x" appears huge at ZONE_MID. The drug isn't in the blood because it's INSIDE the immune cells. Label: "WAIT..."
arc.scene5_proof: The lung fills center frame. A stream of glowing neutrophils (each packed with drug) marches into the infected lung tissue. When each cell reaches bacteria, it bursts open — releasing a concentrated blast of azithromycin shown as expanding rings. The bacteria dissolve on contact. A comparison bar chart at ZONE_LOWER: "BLOOD" bar is tiny (1x), "LUNG TISSUE" bar towers at 98x. Source label at footer: "Trojan horse delivery." Label: "THE PROOF".
arc.scene6_betrayal: The kicker: show a calendar with 5 days crossed off — then the pills STOP. But the neutrophils keep marching into the lung, still glowing, for days and days more. The calendar keeps ticking: day 6, 7, 8, 9, 10... The text "133 HOURS" appears huge — the drug's lung tissue half-life. Your immune cells are still delivering drug almost a WEEK after you stop taking pills. Label: "THE TRUTH".

tts_script: Azithromycin is one of the most prescribed antibiotics on Earth. But here's the thing — only thirty-seven percent of it actually reaches your blood. That's terrible. Most drugs would be useless at that number. So doctors tried the obvious fix: bigger doses, more pills. Didn't help. The drug just vanished from the bloodstream. Then researchers discovered something no one expected. The drug wasn't disappearing. It was hiding — inside your own immune cells. Neutrophils, the white blood cells that rush to infections, were absorbing azithromycin like sponges. Concentrating it sixty to ninety-eight times higher than blood levels. Then carrying it directly into infected tissue and releasing it like a payload. Your immune system wasn't just fighting the bacteria. It was the drug's delivery truck. And here's the wildest part — those cells keep delivering the drug for almost a week after you stop taking the pills.
